Flood Insurance Data

Flood damage over building coverage: NFIP claims by county

In plain words

Of paid claims on NFIP (federal flood insurance) policies for single-family primary homes, with damage and coverage recorded (losses 2016–2025), 4.9% recorded more building damage than the policy's building coverage. In the median listed county it was 2.1%.

Find your county. 268 counties are listed. A county with fewer than 100 of these claims is not listed.

FEMA's records hold 303,311 paid single-family primary-home claims with recorded damage and coverage for losses 2016–2025, across all U.S. counties. In the 268 counties with at least 100 of these claims, 4.9% had recorded building damage over the building coverage (90% range 3.9–5.8%, resampling counties).

By Michael Woo, publisher of Flood Insurance Data (about the site), who works with data, is not an insurance agent, adjuster or engineer, and answers for every figure here. Written with AI tools; every row is recomputed from FEMA's records by a separate check before publishing. First published 2026-11-13; data as of August 31, 2026.

Abstract

Data: 268 counties with at least 100 paid single-family primary-home claims with recorded damage and coverage each (273,450 in all), from FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Claims v3, losses 2016–2025, as of August 31, 2026.

Result: The median county's share is 2.1%; the highest is Humphreys County, TN at 52.4% (54 of 103), and the lowest share, 0.0%, is shared by 21 counties. In the highest county, over half of those 54 claims are from one loss year, 2021, which may hold one flood or several (104 of the 268 counties have at least 10 such claims with one year holding over half).

Question

In which U.S. counties did FEMA's recorded building damage on paid flood claims most often exceed the policy's building coverage, and by how much? The measure is the share of paid single-family primary-home NFIP claims whose recorded building damage (FEMA's actual cash value) was more than the policy's building coverage.

Data

FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Claims v3 (API) records as of August 31, 2026, FEMA fields buildingDamageAmount, totalBuildingInsuranceCoverage, netBuildingPaymentAmount, yearOfLoss, occupancyType, primaryResidenceIndicator, condominiumCoverageTypeCode, nonPaymentReasonBuilding, countyCode. Base: claims with a loss in the window on single-family primary homes (FEMA occupancy type 1 or 11, primary residence, not a condominium coverage type). Each has a building payment above $0, recorded building damage above $0 and building coverage above $0. Here a claim counts as paid on its building payment alone. Records FEMA coded deleted or assigned in error are left out.

FEMA defines buildingDamageAmount as "The actual cash value amount of damage to a main property in whole dollars."

FEMA defines totalBuildingInsuranceCoverage as "Total Insurance Amount in whole dollars on the Building".

Methods

A county's share is how many of these claims had recorded building damage over the building coverage, out of all of these claims in the county FEMA codes on the record, both counted from the same records. Left out: 1,981 counties with fewer than 100 of these claims and 778 with none. In the 1,981 left-out counties with at least one, the median share of damage over building coverage is 0.0% and the pooled share 5.0%, so the listed counties are not a sample of every county. Intervals, fifths, the county-resampling range, records left out and why no test is run: shared methods for every paper.

Results

  • Pooled over the 268 counties: 4.9% (90% range 3.9–5.8%) of 273,450 paid single-family primary-home claims with recorded damage and coverage; the 1,981 counties left out pool to 5.0%.
  • Median county: 2.1%. Highest: Humphreys County, TN, 52.4% (90% range 44.4–60.4%).
  • 10 of the 50 counties with the highest share of damage over building coverage are in Texas, which has 28 of the 268 listed counties.

Prior work

No published ranking of this measure by county was found in searches on 2026-11-12 (WebSearch: NFIP claims damage exceeded coverage by county).

Limitations

  • Damage over coverage compares FEMA's recorded actual cash value with the building coverage on the policy; it is not the owner's uninsured loss, which also depends on contents, deductibles, replacement cost, other insurance and aid.
  • Only insured, paid claims are in the base: homes without flood insurance are not.
  • A marked row has at least 10 claims over coverage with one loss year holding over half of them. That year may hold one flood or several. Claims from one flood are not independent, so a marked county's 90% range is narrower than it should be.
  • Counties are those FEMA codes on the claim, which can differ from the property's county.
  • Only NFIP records: private flood insurance is not in FEMA's data.
  • A fifth is a position in this list, not a grade, a risk score or a prediction.

Reproduce

Download every record from FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Claims v3, keep the paid single-family primary-home claims with recorded damage and coverage for losses 2016–2025 and group them by the county FEMA codes, dropping counties under 100. Compute each share of damage over building coverage with a 90% Wilson interval (z = 1.64485) and check it against the CSV, which gives every numerator and denominator.

How to cite

Michael Woo, Flood Insurance Data, "Flood damage over building coverage: NFIP claims by county," NFIP losses 2016–2025, data as of August 31, 2026, https://floodinsurancedata.com/flood-insurance/damage-over-coverage/. This product uses FEMA's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Versions

Data as of August 31, 2026 (current), kept at its own dated address with its CSV. This is the first version. Each data refresh adds a new dated version; earlier versions are not changed.

No corrections so far. Report a figure that looks wrong to contact@floodinsurancedata.com; every correction is listed here with its date.
